title: Master Guide to Confusing English Grammar Usage (A vs B)

a0_a2.core_difference: Use 'a' before consonant sounds; use 'an' before vowel sounds.
a0_a2.usage_a: Use 'a' when the next word begins with a consonant sound (e.g. a car, a university /j-sound/).
a0_a2.usage_b: Use 'an' when the next word begins with a vowel sound (e.g. an apple, an hour /silent h/).
examples: I bought a car yesterday.
She has an apple in her bag.
He studied at a university.
We waited for an hour.
a0_a2.quick_logic: Listen to the first sound, not the first letter.
a0_a2.memory_trick: Sound determines the article: Vowel sound = AN, Consonant sound = A.

a0_a2.point: a / an vs the vs zero article (Ø)
a0_a2.core_difference: a/an = non-specific singular countable; the = specific/known; Ø = general plural/uncountable.
a0_a2.usage_a: Use a/an when introducing something for the first time or any one of a category.
a0_a2.usage_b: Use the when both speaker and listener know exactly which specific item is meant.
examples: I saw a dog in the park.
The dog was barking at me.
Ø Dogs are loyal animals.
a0_a2.quick_logic: Ask 'Which one?' → If clear, use THE. If general/any, use A/AN or Ø.
common_mistakes: ❌ I like the dogs in general. → ✓ I like dogs.
a0_a2.memory_trick: First time = A/AN, Second time = THE.

a0_a2.core_difference: Present Simple = habits, routines, facts. Present Continuous = actions happening right now or temporary situations.
a0_a2.usage_a: Present Simple for permanent truths and regular habits (always, usually, every day).
a0_a2.usage_b: Present Continuous for active events happening right now or temporary phases (this week, currently).
examples: She works in London.
She is working from home this week.
Water boils at 100°C.
common_mistakes: ❌ I am knowing him. → ✓ I know him. (Stative verbs don't take continuous)

a0_a2.core_difference: Past Simple = finished action in a finished time. Present Perfect = past action connected to the present.
a0_a2.usage_a: Past Simple with specific finished time markers (yesterday, last year, in 2020, ago).
a0_a2.usage_b: Present Perfect for life experiences, unfinished time (today, this week), or present results.
examples: I visited Rome in 2019.
I have visited Rome three times.
She lost her keys yesterday.
She has lost her keys (she doesn't have them now).
a0_a2.quick_logic: Finished time word? → Past Simple. Connection to now? → Present Perfect.
common_mistakes: ❌ I have seen him yesterday. → ✓ I saw him yesterday.
a0_a2.memory_trick: Yesterday closes the door (Past Simple). Present Perfect keeps the door open.

a0_a2.core_difference: Will = instant decisions/promises/predictions. Going to = prior plans/intentions & evidence-based predictions.
a0_a2.usage_a: Use 'will' when deciding on the spot or offering help.
a0_a2.usage_b: Use 'going to' when a plan was made before speaking or when present evidence points to the outcome.
examples: The phone is ringing. I'll get it!
Look at those dark clouds! It's going to rain.
We are going to buy a new car next month.
a0_a2.quick_logic: Decided now? → WILL. Decided before / Evidence now? → GOING TO.
common_mistakes: ❌ I decided yesterday. I will visit him tomorrow. → ✓ I am going to visit him.
a0_a2.memory_trick: Will = Instant Spark. Going to = Pre-planned Path.

b1_b2.core_difference: Past Continuous = background action in progress. Past Simple = interrupting event.
b1_b2.usage_a: Past Continuous sets the background scene (was walking, were studying).
b1_b2.usage_b: Past Simple expresses completed actions that happen in sequence or interrupt.
examples: I was cooking dinner when the phone rang.
While we were sleeping, it started to snow.
b1_b2.quick_logic: Long background action = Continuous. Short interrupting event = Simple.
common_mistakes: ❌ When I was arriving, he spoke. → ✓ When I arrived, he was speaking.
b1_b2.memory_trick: Continuous is the movie background, Simple is the sudden strike.

b1_b2.point: Used to vs Would (Past Habits & States)
b1_b2.core_difference: Used to works for both past states and habits. Would ONLY works for repeated past actions.
b1_b2.usage_a: Used to for past states (live, have, be, like) and repeated past actions that no longer happen.
b1_b2.usage_b: Would for repeated nostalgic past actions only (never for past states).
examples: I used to live in Paris. (State)
Every summer, we would go camping by the lake. (Repeated action)
b1_b2.quick_logic: State verb (live, be, have)? → MUST use Used to. Action verb? → Can use Used to or Would.
common_mistakes: ❌ I would live in London when I was young. → ✓ I used to live in London.
b1_b2.memory_trick: Would needs action; Used to takes both state and action.

b1_b2.core_difference: 1st = real future; 2nd = unreal present/hypothetical; 3rd = unreal past regret.
b1_b2.usage_a: 1st Conditional (If + Present, Will + V): real future possibilities.
b1_b2.usage_b: 2nd Conditional (If + Past Simple, Would + V): imaginary/unreal present situations.
b1_b2.usage_c: 3rd Conditional (If + Past Perfect, Would have + V3): unreal past events that cannot change.
examples: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home. (1st)
If I won the lottery today, I would buy an island. (2nd)
If I had studied harder last year, I would have passed the exam. (3rd)
b1_b2.quick_logic: Real future = 1st. Unreal present = 2nd. Unreal past = 3rd.
common_mistakes: ❌ If I would win, I will buy... → ✓ If I win, I will buy...
b1_b2.memory_trick: Step back in time for higher irreality: Present → Past → Past Perfect.

b1_b2.core_difference: Defining = essential information (no commas, 'that' allowed). Non-defining = extra info (commas required, no 'that').
b1_b2.usage_a: Defining relative clauses identify exactly which person or thing is being talked about.
b1_b2.usage_b: Non-defining relative clauses add extra commentary that could be dropped without breaking core meaning.
examples: The car that I bought last week is very fast. (Defining)
My brother, who lives in Sydney, is a doctor. (Non-defining)
b1_b2.quick_logic: Drop the clause: does the sentence lose its identity? If yes → Defining (no commas). If no → Non-defining (commas).
common_mistakes: ❌ My father, that is 60, retired. → ✓ My father, who is 60, retired.
b1_b2.memory_trick: Commas hug extra information. 'That' hates commas!
